analysis.one_liner: Sets enforceable standards for immigrant detention and phases out private detention facilities.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 11 cosponsors and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which has taken no further action on it.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would set enforceable minimum standards for every facility where immigrants are held by the Department of Homeland Security, with unannounced annual inspections, public reports, fines for failures, and a right for detained people to sue over violations. It would end mandatory detention by requiring a hearing before an immigration judge within days of arrest, starting from a presumption of release, and it would ban detaining children in ICE facilities and ban solitary confinement. It would also phase out for-profit detention within three years, replacing it with government-run facilities and community-based supervision run by nonprofits.
analysis.who_benefits: Immigrants held in DHS custody and their families gain enforceable living standards, prompt custody hearings before a judge, a presumption of release, protection from solitary confinement, an end to child detention in ICE facilities, and the right to sue in federal court when standards are violated. Nonprofit community organizations gain new contracts for case management and legal orientation services. The public gains transparency: public inspection reports, a monthly public list of every facility and its compliance status, 60-day public reports on deaths in custody, and members of Congress allowed into any facility without advance notice.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Homeland Security Secretary to write binding detention standards, at minimum matching the American Bar Association's civil immigration detention standards, for every facility holding immigrants, updated at least every two years.

Directs the DHS Inspector General to make unannounced, in-person inspections of every detention facility at least annually and post the results publicly; facilities that fail are fined at least 10% of their contract value, and repeat failures force detainees to be moved and the contract terminated.

Replaces mandatory detention with due process: an initial custody decision within 48 hours, a hearing before an immigration judge within 72 hours, a presumption of release that the government must rebut with clear and convincing evidence, bonds set at an amount the detainee can actually pay, and no detention solely because someone cannot afford bond.

Bans detaining anyone under 18 in an ICE-operated or contracted facility, bans solitary confinement outright, and requires a probable-cause hearing within 48 hours of a warrantless arrest, with interrogation barred from being based on race, ethnicity, language, or similar traits.

Ends for-profit detention: within three years, no ICE contracts with private prison companies or jails, and all detention facilities must be owned and operated by the government, with for-profit monitoring programs replaced by community-based case management run by nonprofits at no cost to participants.

Opens the system to public view: monthly public data on every facility (beds, population, compliance status, length of stay), public reports within 60 days of any death in custody with a medical root-cause analysis, detention contracts made subject to public records requests, and members of Congress allowed to enter any facility without advance notice.
Lets a detained person who is injured by a violation of the standards sue in federal court for injunctive relief and compensatory damages, with attorney fees for the winning side.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers bear the cost of the transition: the government must own and operate all detention facilities within three years, meaning building or acquiring capacity currently leased from private companies and local jails, and funding a new community-based case management program. Private prison companies and local jails lose their ICE detention contracts, and for-profit electronic-monitoring providers lose the alternatives-to-detention business. Federal contractors that fail inspections face fines of at least 10% of their contract value.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers; private prison firms lose contracts

drawbacks.text: The three-year phase-out requires the government to own and operate all detention capacity, which means major new construction and staffing costs for taxpayers and could leave the government short of beds in the interim unless it releases or transfers people quickly.

The ban on solitary confinement is absolute, with no exception for separating a detainee who is violent or a danger to cellmates; an honest supporter must acknowledge that facilities would lose any segregation tool and would have to manage dangerous situations by transfer or staffing instead.

The bill bans ankle monitors and other electronic surveillance as an alternative to detention, removing a supervision tool that costs far less than either detention or the bill's community case management program; opponents would argue this makes the alternative system more expensive without clear added benefit.

A presumption of release with bonds set to what a person can afford means more people await their hearings outside custody; opponents would argue this raises the risk of non-appearance, though the bill still allows detention when the government proves by clear and convincing evidence that someone is a danger or will flee.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protections — binding standards, unannounced inspections, public reporting of deaths, prompt custody hearings, and a right to sue — respond to a system that today runs largely on unenforceable contract standards, and they are cheap relative to what the government already spends on detention. The expensive and genuinely contested parts are the forced three-year exit from private facilities and jails, which shifts building and operating costs onto taxpayers, and the combination of a release presumption with a ban on ankle monitors, which moves the system toward community supervision at public expense. The bill is ambitious but internally coherent; the honest trade-off is higher transparency and rights for detainees in exchange for higher direct public costs and less flexible facility management.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee on January 27, 2026, and the committee has not held a hearing or vote on it since; the bill is still technically alive while this Congress runs through early January 2027.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the bill on January 27, 2026, joined by 10 Democratic senators and one independent, Senator Sanders.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day, which is the normal first step; it has had no hearing, markup, or vote since.
With 11 cosponsors out of 100 senators, no Republican support, and the bill sitting in committee, it has not advanced in the roughly a year remaining before this Congress ends on January 3, 2027.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won yet, because nothing has happened since referral. As of now, private prison companies and local jails keep operating their existing ICE detention contracts while the bill waits in committee.

for.name: Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 11 cosponsors

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Committee has taken no recorded action on the bill since it was referred — no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled

sides.party_line_note: All 12 original sponsors are Democrats or the independent from Vermont; no Republican has cosponsored, and the chamber's 55 Republicans control whether the bill ever gets committee time.

industries.industry: Private prison and for-profit immigration detention operators
industries.note: The bill terminates all for-profit detention contracts within three years and requires detention facilities to be government-owned and operated, and companies like GEO Group and CoreCivic would lose their ICE detention business. Even before the phase-out, repeated failed inspections trigger fines of at least 10% of the contract value and then termination and transfer of all detainees.

industries.industry: For-profit electronic monitoring and alternatives-to-detention providers
industries.note: The bill bans ankle monitors and other electronic surveillance as alternatives to detention and terminates for-profit contracts for monitoring programs, replacing them with community case management run by nonprofits or the government. This eliminates the for-profit ICE monitoring line of business.

industries.industry: Local governments and county jails that house ICE detainees
industries.note: Jail contracts with ICE must be terminated within three years, ending a revenue stream many counties rely on. Communities lose the dollars, though the bill also mandates indoor climate-controlled visitor areas and enforceable standards in the interim.

The bill directs DHS to give contract priority to community-based nonprofits running case management programs, requires a nonprofit-run legal orientation program at every facility, and guarantees detainees confidential access to counsel. Nonprofits become the permanent channel for these services.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding 55 Senate seats and no Republican cosponsor, the bill is unlikely to get a hearing or vote in the Judiciary Committee this session; bills like this typically die when the Congress ends on January 3, 2027, unless attached to a larger package. The realistic path is reintroduction in a future Congress, with support growing or shrinking depending on who controls the chamber.
